title: "Hyperspectral data is big!"
description: "Development trade-off in hyperspectral software"

date: 2026-10-03

---

For a single core box (SWIR data, for this example, as that is what I mostly work with):
- Raw dataset: ~ 400Mb 
- Cropped reflectance: ~170Mb
- Derived data:
 - Smoothed: ~170Mb
 - Normalised: 300Mb
 - Mask, bands, metadata, Interpretation images: ~10Mb 
For a typical project (10-12 holes, ~80 boxes each), that's ~600 GB total. Should I really store all of that?

There are three resources available to a system working with hyperspectral data:
- Disk storage
- Time
- RAM

Time

If I only store cropped reflectance and compute derivatives on-demand, that solves the storage problem, but I pay in time.
To recalculate the smoothing on demand is ~1-2 seconds, to recalculate the continuum removal is ~ 10-30 seconds. 
Lets say we want to try a processing technique on each box in a 200m hole (45 boxes), that is about 25 minutes just in re-deriving the products needed, with whatever time penalty your feature extraction or correlation has added on top.
That is some frustrating processing, difficult to iterate.

RAM

Okay, so for interactive processing, caching would definitely be an advantage. Do I really need it all on disk?

Many of the processes I run require both the smoothed data and the normalised, but lets say our processes just require the normalised. So, lets cache that in RAM at startup, a one-time slowdown, but fast iterative processing experience with no wasted disk space. 

For our 45 box hole, approximately ~300Mb per normalised dataset, that is 13.5Gb of RAM required. At startup. Lets hope our algorithm doesn’t produce any intermediate arrays of any size and that we never work with a hole longer than 200m.

Disk

So, I am back to aggressively caching to disk. It looked wasteful when I started, nearly doubling the size of the data storage just on intermediate products. However, compared to time and RAM, it is by far the most abundant resource.

My strategy of caching everything to disk gives me access to memmaping, which means I can have a 1km hole “open”, over 150Gb of data. By carefully managing dropping a fully read array back to a memmap I can work on a full hole using an 8Gb RAM machine.

What looked extremely wasteful when I started is actually just maximising the most scarce resources.

I am adding architecture for an archive file for long term storage. This will be the minimum dataset to deterministically reproduce the full analysed box.

Other strategies:
- Eliminate the time penalties with more efficient computing?
 - Maybe this has been solved in the commercial software world, but Python gives too much for me to move away from it (NumPy, SciPy, Hylite).
- Solve RAM with very high-end workstations?
 -I do not see a >64Gb RAM machine in my professional near-future, and certainly not a >128Gb.
